cards.explanation: The answer is a centurion named Julius. Julius is a centurion, a Roman officer, and he belongs to the Imperial Regiment. Paul and the other prisoners are handed over to him (Acts 27:1). From here on, he's the one watching over them. Paul just got a new boss, friends.

The answer is True. At Sidon, Julius "…treated Paul with consideration, allowing him to visit his friends and receive their care." (Acts 27:3). Paul is still a prisoner, but a friendly stop is a friendly stop. Say what you want about a long trip, a visit with friends makes it better.

The answer is winds. They sail to the lee of Cyprus "…because the winds were against us." (Acts 27:4). The lee is the side that blocks the wind, so the island helps shield them. It's like ducking around the corner of a building when the wind hits you right in the face.

The answer is Alexandria. At Myra, Julius finds an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and puts them on board (Acts 27:6). That's the ship that finally goes where they're headed. It's like waiting forever at the stop and the right bus finally rolls up with Italy on the sign.

The answer is False. On this trip to Italy, they move along the coast of Crete "with difficulty" before they come to Fair Havens (Acts 27:8). The wind has already been against them earlier on the trip. So Crete is no free ride, friends.

The answer is disaster and great loss, even of their lives. At Fair Havens, Paul says, "Men, I can see that our voyage will be filled with disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well." (Acts 27:10). That's a serious warning, and he gives it plainly. He names the ship, the cargo and the people on board.

The answer is False. "…contrary to Paul’s advice, the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship." (Acts 27:11). Julius hears Paul, but he follows the other two. I'd be a little nervous right about here, friends.

The answer is the pilot. The centurion "…was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship." (Acts 27:11). The text puts it just like that: contrary to Paul's advice, those two are the ones who persuaded him. Paul's advice is the one he went against.

The answer is that the harbor isn't good for spending winter. The text says "…the harbor was unsuitable to winter in…" so the majority decided to sail on (Acts 27:12). They're hoping to reach Phoenix, another harbor on Crete. It's a plan with a reason, friends, even if it's the one that went against Paul.

The answer is a cyclone called the Northeaster. "…a cyclone called the Northeaster swept down across the island." (Acts 27:14). The gentle south wind didn't last long. One verse it's calm, and the next verse it's a cyclone.
The answer is False. As they pass the small island of Cauda, the text says "…we barely managed to secure the lifeboat." (Acts 27:16). That's a tough job in a storm. They get it done, but only just.

The answer is that they pass ropes under the ship. After the lifeboat is hoisted, the crew "…used ropes to undergird the ship." (Acts 27:17). That means they wrapped ropes around it to hold it together. A ship in a storm needs all the help it can get.

The answer is True. "On the third day, they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands." (Acts 27:19). The day before, they'd begun tossing the cargo (Acts 27:18). Now they're throwing gear over too. When you start tossing the ship's own equipment, the storm has your full attention.

The answer is that they lose all hope of being saved. The text says "…we abandoned all hope of being saved." (Acts 27:20). No sun, no stars for many days, and the storm still battering them. I think this one hurts.

The answer is that they should have taken his advice and stayed. Standing among the men in the storm, Paul says, "Men, you should have followed my advice not to sail from Crete. Then you would have averted this disaster and loss." (Acts 27:21). He puts that out there first. Then he moves on to what comes next.

The answer is True. Paul says, "…you will not experience any loss of life, but only of the ship." (Acts 27:22). Think about how that lands after days of no hope. That's why he says to keep up their courage.

The answer is the ship. Paul says there will be no loss of life, "…but only of the ship." (Acts 27:22). The cargo and tackle are already going over the side (Acts 27:18-19). The loss of life is the thing Paul says won't happen.

The answer is stand before Caesar. The angel who stood beside Paul says, "Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar." (Acts 27:24). The angel also says God has granted him the lives of all who sail with him. So Paul has somewhere to be, storm or no storm.

The answer is False. Paul says, "However, we must run aground on some island." (Acts 27:26). That fits with what he said earlier, that the loss would be the ship (Acts 27:22). Safe lives, a lost ship, and a lot of story still ahead.
